characters: Lamiokor: a 13-year-old girl with neat braids in a purple JHS uniform, holding a smartphone.
Prince: Lamiokor’s classmate, 14, tall, in the same uniform, usually fast with his thumbs.
The class prefect: a calm 14-year-old with a badge on his shirt.
The headteacher: a woman in a navy suit who signs the notice at the school gate.

narrationPlan.voice: Natural teenage voices; Lamiokor is calm and curious; the voice note itself is read in an urgent, anonymous tone
narrationPlan.pace: Brisk but clear, with a calm turn at the end (about 130 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quiet synth pulse with a subtle notification chime, resolving into warm piano (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Class WhatsApp-style groups and forwarded voice notes are a normal part of many Ghanaian students’ lives; Lamiokor is a traditional Ga name. The story is set in a fictional school, with a fictional incident, to avoid alarming readers with a real event.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Is it clear that the outbreak is fictional and the message is false?
Does the story avoid shaming Prince?

teacherGuide.overview: A media-literacy story where students, not an expert, work out how to verify a message and show kindness to the classmate who shared it. The teacher’s role is to run the follow-up.
learningGoals: Identify signs that a message may be unreliable.
Use three checking questions before sharing.
Respond to mistakes with kindness and honesty.
beforeReading: Ask: have you ever received a message you were not sure about?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to name the missing details themselves.
afterReading: Give learners three mock messages (invented by the teacher) and ask them to check them with the three questions.
discussion: Why did the message ask to be forwarded quickly?
What helped Prince admit his mistake?
reflection: What is your own rule for checking a message before sharing it?

support: Provide a checklist with the three questions.
stretch: Write a short script of a calm reply that could be posted in a group when a doubtful message appears.

culturalNotes: Class WhatsApp-style groups and forwarded voice notes are a normal part of many Ghanaian students’ lives; Lamiokor is a traditional Ga name. The story is set in a fictional school, with a fictional incident, to avoid alarming readers with a real event.
localiseThis: Adapt to the platforms your learners actually use.
Use invented examples, never real alarming news or real people.

reviewerNotes: Confirm Ga vowel and final open o (ɔ).
